item.title: Commentary The Table Is the Point: Transparency, Dialogue and Why a Small Town Still Needs Independent Press
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — On the first day of September, roughly sixty people filled a room at Otero Arts and more than 700 hundred more have watched online as City Manager Robert Stockwell explained, to a public that had not been asked, why the city was considering up to a million dollars in fencing at Bonito Lake and an end to public fishing access. Sitting on the same panel or in the same room were the mayor, three commissioners, a former mayor, a former city manager, the mayors of Ruidoso and Ruidoso Downs, the county's chief executive and the Department of Game and Fish and more. 

At the event the proposal had changed. Mr. Stockwell put forward a five-point plan that keeps fishing access, fences only the dam and its ancillary structures, and opens a six-month review with the state, both counties and the Village of Ruidoso. The Commission votes on September 22, 2026.

I want to dwell on that for a moment, because it is the whole argument for a small-town press in one evening. Nobody sued anyone. Nobody filed a records request seeking answers. A conversation and a decision that was drifting toward a consent agenda was pulled into a room with the people it affected, and it got better. 

That is what transparency is actually for. It is not a procedural hobby. It is the difference between a policy made about a community and a policy made with one.

Readers have noticed, and some have asked pointedly, why Mr. Stockwell keeps showing up to our platforms. He gave this outlet via the radio edition with Anthony Lucero his first interview after his appointment. He sat on our Bonito Lake panel and has others. Meanwhile I am the petitioner in Edwards v. Alamogordo City Commission, a case that argues the process that put him in the job violated the Open Meetings Act.

Both things are true, and neither one embarrasses me. The lawsuit has never been about Mr. Stockwell's résumé or his character. It is about how a unanimous 7–0 vote in March to negotiate a contract with Dr. Stephanie Hernandez became, within weeks and with little public explanation, a $485,340 taxpayer-funded separation, and a 5–2 appointment of a man who told KALH listeners, he was first approached about the job "probably last July 2025" — nearly a year before the vote. Those are questions about certain Commissioners conduct, not about the manager's competence.

"A journalist who will only interview people he agrees with is not a journalist. A city manager who will only talk to outlets that flatter him is not much of a public servant. Mr. Stockwell has chosen the harder path, and I respect it." - Chris Edwards

Mr. Stockwell, for his part, could have stonewalled the loudest critic of the process that hired him. Plenty of officials would have. Instead he walked into our microphones, took the questions and, at Bonito Lake, listened to a room that disagreed with him. That is what professional administration looks like, and residents deserve to see it regardless of what I think about the meeting that produced his contract.

The criticism that arrives in my inbox from the other direction deserves an honest answer too. It goes like this: Edwards runs a segment with the former city manager, publishes a sworn statement from the former mayor, has a working relationship with the sitting mayor, and now hosts the current city manager. Isn't that just an insiders' club with a website?

Here is the record. Alamogordo Town News was sharply critical of Susan Payne's administration when she held the gavel especially early in her administration.  Dr. Hernandez's new segment, "The Doctor Is In," which debuted last week, is labeled as commentary and analysis from a former administrator, not as news reporting, and readers can weigh it accordingly. Mayor McDonald's votes and statements are covered the same way everyone else's are; when she is right on process, we say so, and when the record says otherwise, we say that too.

What ties these people together is not friendship. It is that each of them has been willing to put a name and, in some cases, a signature under oath behind what they know about how this city is run. That is the only currency this newsroom accepts. Commissioners Stephen Burnett and Al Hernandez, both of whom voted for the Stockwell contract, were in the audience at Otero Arts on September 1, alongside Mayor McDonald and Commissioner Warren Robinson, who voted against it. That is to their credit — all of them. The standing invitation to every commissioner is to do the same thing on the microphone, on the record, about the process itself. That invitation remains open.

There is a reason cities the size of Alamogordo are where local journalism died first. The economics are brutal. Government is close, personal and quick to retaliate. And it is genuinely uncomfortable to report on people you will see at the grocery store.

But it is also where a press is most necessary, because the substitutes do not exist. There is no statehouse bureau watching the Alamogordo City Commission. There is no wire service at the executive session door. When the Commission's own outside counsel, in a filing to a federal agency, acknowledged that a round of city manager interviews had been conducted in a manner inconsistent with the Open Meetings Act, that fact did not surface through a press release. It surfaced through an Inspection of Public Records Act request that took months to be released into the public domain.

The Murillo recall petition against Commissioner Burnett was dismissed on September 9, and the City has now asked the court to throw out the Open Meetings Act case as well. Those are the courts doing their job, and I will argue my side in the proper forum as my case continues. 

But no ruling on probable cause or on a motion to dismiss changes what the documents already show: that a decision was made, then unmade, and that the public was told little in between. 

A community's right to know how its money and its leadership were disposed of does not depend on whether a judge finds a statutory violation, it depends on a free and vibrant press.

So here is the compact this outlet operates under to officials and readers alike.

To the Commission: come to the table. Not to our table specifically — any table with the public at it. Hold the discussion in the open before the vote, not the press conference after it, or hiding behind executive sessions. The Bonito Lake episode proved that daylight improves decisions. It did not weaken the city manager; it strengthened his plan.

To readers: hold us to the same standard. When this newsroom gets a fact wrong, prove it with documentation and we will correct it in print. We had an error in a story earlier today, the city manager corrected us and we posted his response to correct immediately.  Most every affidavit, IPRA response, or contract or source we cite is posted so you can read the source rather than take our word for it.

A small town does not need a press that is neutral about transparency. It needs one that is relentless about it, and that applies that relentlessness to its own allies. 

The measure of whether we succeed is not who sits at the table. It is whether the door was open when they sat down.

Chris Edwards is editor in chief of Alamogordo Town News and 2nd Life Media and hosts on KALH Radio. He is the petitioner in Edwards v. Alamogordo City Commission, No. D-1215-CV-2026-00514, Twelfth Judicial District Court. Commentary reflects the opinion of the author.

item.title: PRC Plans Alamogordo Public Meeting on PNM Billing Concerns
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission is finalizing plans to hold a public meeting in Alamogordo to hear directly from residents about electric billing problems with PNM. The commission has approached local government officials about hosting the event, though local government is unaffiliated with the issue, tentatively scheduled for Tuesday, September 29, from noon to 2 p.m.

Area state representatives are expected to take part, along with Sen. Jim Townsend, the Republican who has represented Senate District 34 since January 2025. The PRC says it will issue a formal press release within the next few days confirming the venue and other details as an official public notice.

Residents should treat the time and format as tentative until then.

Why the meeting is happening

The session follows weeks of frustration over unusually high summer electric bills and pressure from the press, local officials and the public.. According to the PRC, the complaints it has received have come mainly from customers in the Alamogordo area, beginning in July. The root cause, PNM says, was a meter reader shortage that forced the utility to estimate electric use, leaving tens of thousands of customers with bigger bills.

Locally, PNM reports 8,764 meters in the area, many of which were placed on estimated or delayed billing after the company began estimating reads on July 21; allegedly customers weren't notified until August 3, about two weeks later. Because reads were delayed, many households received a single bill covering two months of summer power. Some customers say that combination pushed them into higher-priced usage tiers. Multiple Alamogordo resident told state investigators that PNM overestimated their usage in June and July, and that the estimates plus the 60-day billing cycle drove their accounts into a higher rate tiers.

Growing pressure on the utility

The billing issue has drawn attention well beyond city hall. Mayor Sharon McDonald contacted PNM leadership directly, stressing that the problems were systematic rather than isolated customer service complaints. In September, Attorney General Raúl Torrez's office hand-delivered a letter to Don Tarry, president and CEO of PNM's parent company TXNM Energy, asking the utility to explain its billing practices. That letter listed at least 16 similar complaints filed with the state Department of Justice.

PNM has apologized and says it has essentially caught up on missed meter reads and does not expect further estimated bills. The utility has also suspended late fees and disconnections for nonpayment for all affected customers, and it hosted customer assistance events in Alamogordo in August and again on September 12. Still, the PRC has said customers may continue to see unusual bills due to estimation or delayed billing, that the situation is highly concerning to the commission, and that it is weighing whether further action is needed.

How to prepare

Residents planning to attend or comment should bring copies of recent bills, any notices from PNM about estimated readings, and past bills from the same months in prior years for comparison. Watch for the PRC's official notice later this week for the confirmed location and instructions on signing up to speak. Stay turned for an official release from the PRC for specifics

item.title: Alamogordo Cross Country Girls Take Third, Boys Seventh at NMMI Invitational
item.description:
ROSWELL — The Alamogordo girls cross country team placed third and the boys finished seventh at Saturday's NMMI Invitational, hosted by New Mexico Military Institute.

The Lady Tigers were led by a strong one-two punch up front. Aurora Van Beusichem crossed the line third overall in 20:30.72, and teammate Alex Simmons was right behind her in fourth at 20:41.83, giving Alamogordo two top-five finishers in the girls varsity race.

Adalynn Chavez was the team's third runner, placing 21st in 21:57.99. Nizhoni Castillo (26th, 22:40.00) and Jocelyn Pittman (28th, 22:43.53) finished just three seconds apart to round out the scoring five, a tight pack that helped secure the podium team finish. Genesis Sayas (41st, 24:33.25) and Siena Cass (45th, 25:08.66) also ran for the Lady Tigers.

On the boys side, Zachary Swayzee led Alamogordo with a 19th-place finish in 17:45.29 in a varsity field of 72 finishers on the 5K course. Kellen Casebolt was next for the Tigers in 44th (19:46.09), followed by a closely bunched group of Nickolas Starkovich (48th, 20:25.24), Austin Amberson (50th, 20:28.11) and Calvin Khan (51st, 20:39.81). Chase Bailey placed 59th in 21:43.79. Hagerman's Fernando Zamora won the boys race in 15:42.

Alamogordo returns to action Friday at the Volcano Vista Meet in Albuquerque.

item.title: Centennial Sweeps Alamogordo in District Soccer Openers
item.description:
Centennial opened district play with a pair of lopsided wins over Alamogordo, as the Hawks' girls cruised 8-0 and the boys pulled away for a 5-0 victory.

In the boys' match, the Tigers held Centennial scoreless through the first 20 minutes before the Hawks broke through. Solomon Rogosta scored in the 21st minute to give Centennial a 1-0 lead, then converted a penalty kick later in the half to send the Hawks into halftime up 2-0.

Centennial extended its lead in the second half when Ignacio Hernandez scored in the 63rd minute to make it 3-0. The Hawks then struck twice in quick succession, with Christian Frank scoring in the 73rd minute and Andres Cardenas adding another a minute later to seal the 5-0 final.

The loss drops the Tigers to 3-6-2 overall and 0-1 in district play. Alamogordo will look to rebound Thursday when it travels to Organ Mountain.

The Lady Tigers had a difficult night of their own, falling 8-0 to a strong Centennial squad. The defeat moves Alamogordo to 2-8-1 overall and 0-1 in district. The Lady Tigers return home Thursday to host Organ Mountain.

item.title: City Leadership Gives Two Different Accounts of How the Al Hernandez Complaint Was Handled
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO N.M. — On Monday, City Manager Robert Stockwell said the Code of Conduct complaint against Commissioner Alfonso "Al" Hernandez was handled entirely by the city's former attorney, now working on contract. On Tuesday, he said the attorney only checked the paperwork.

Stockwell's first statement came in a comment to Alamogordo Town News on Sept. 21 at 9 a.m.: "The entire matter was handled by Darrell Mori through the firm, Virtue Law. My only role was to distribute the forms and instructions to the Commissioners and place the item on the agenda."

At 8:51 a.m. Tuesday, hours before the Commission votes on the complaint, Stockwell emailed ATN a different description, when pressed by the journalist for more details. The municipal code, he wrote, "directs the City Attorney to determine whether the complaint 'complies with the requirements of subsection (b)(4)c.' Darrell Mori, as Legal Counsel to the City, determined that the complaint complied and the complaint was sent to the three-member preliminary review committee. It does not direct the City Attorney to conduct an investigation."

Read together, the two statements confirm what Alamogordo Town News initially reported,  no one outside investigated the allegations. A contract attorney checked the complaint's form. Three commissioners read it. Tonight, the remaining commissioners will vote on whether anyone should look further.

A city attorney's job, with no city attorney

The code within the city charter assigns the first step to "the City Attorney." Alamogordo has not had one since May, when Mori resigned from the post. He left to pursue private practice in northern New Mexico and received a settlement from the city on his departure. He now provides legal services to the city on contract through his firm, Virtue Law.

Stockwell told the Commission in late August that a search for a replacement had produced one applicant he chose not to hire, that he would try "one more time" with a month-long search, and that if it failed he would recommend contracting out the city's legal work altogether. Asked by a commissioner what they could do to help, he answered, "pray," the Alamogordo Daily News reported Aug. 29.

Stockwell's Tuesday email is careful on this point: it describes Mori as "Legal Counsel to the City," not as City Attorney. Whether a contract lawyer's sign-off satisfies a code provision that names the City Attorney, and whether the city's former attorney, paid a settlement to leave four months ago, is the right person to screen a complaint against a sitting commissioner, are questions the city has not addressed and raises further questions. 

The process, as the city describes it

The complaint, filed by a city employee, is the first ever processed under Section 2-03-570 of the Alamogordo Municipal Code, according to Stockwell. Under that section, a complaint against a commissioner goes first to the City Attorney for a compliance check, then to a Preliminary Review Committee made up of the three most senior commissioners, who review the complaint and any response from the accused commissioner individually.

According to the agenda report for Item No. 10, two of the three committee members found "No Cause" on all four counts and the third found "Cause" on all four. Because of the split, the full Commission decides whether the complaint proceeds. The motion needs five affirmative votes; Hernandez cannot vote. If it falls short, the agenda report states, "no further action on the complaint may be taken."

The agenda packet does not describe the allegations. The city has not said which commissioners sat on the committee or how each voted.

"Apples to oranges"

Stockwell rejected any comparison to the city's handling of earlier disputes involving commissioners. In 2023 and 2025, the Commission and City Attorney commissioned investigations into allegations of commissioner interference raised by a former city manager and into then-Acting City Manager Dr. Stephanie Hernandez's allegations of bias in the city manager hiring process. Mori was City Attorney during both.

"Conflating the current complaint with actions taken by the City Commission and City Attorney in 2023 and 2025 ... is comparing apples to oranges," Stockwell wrote. "In neither of these instances was a complaint filed using Section 2-3-570."

He acknowledged the current process has critics. "While legal minds and others may feel the current process should involve an independent investigation there is nothing in the Section 2-03-570 process that envisions such an investigation," he wrote. "Whether the current process in the code is the best way to handle complaints of Code of Conduct violations, it is a discussion for another time. The City has an obligation to the employee who filed the complaint to see it through in full accordance with the Municipal Code."

What the law allows the public to see

The city has treated the substance of the complaint as confidential. New Mexico law does not obviously support that. The Inspection of Public Records Act exempts "matters of opinion in personnel files," but the Court of Appeals in Cox v. New Mexico Department of Public Safety (2010) limited that exemption to records about the employer-employee relationship, and held that complaints about a public official's conduct in office are public even when filed in a personnel file. Hernandez is an elected official, not a city employee; the city is not his employer.

The Open Meetings Act likewise allows a public body to close a meeting only for "limited personnel matters" involving "any individual public employee." A complaint against an elected commissioner does not fit that description, and the vote itself, as a final action, must be taken in public regardless.

ATN filed a public records request Tuesday seeking the complaint, Mori's compliance determination, the forms and instructions distributed to the committee, each committee member's findings on each count, any communications among the three members or with Stockwell, Mori, Virtue Law, or Hernandez, and any invoices or billing from Virtue Law for work on the matter. The city's response is due in about 15 days.

Tonight

The Commission meets at 6:30 p.m. in the Donald E. Carroll City Commission Chambers at City Hall, 1376 E. Ninth St. Item 10 asks the six eligible commissioners whether the allegations against their colleague will be examined at all. Two of those six, presumably, already voted "No Cause" as members of the committee.

Whatever the outcome, the vote will not determine whether the allegations are true. Under the code as Stockwell describes it, that question has not yet been asked. ATN will release further details post tonights vote and after the IPRA or public information request has been fulfilled. Stay tuned...

item.title: Crises at the Lincoln County Jail Left Without a Medical Provider with Detainees on Suicide Watch
item.description:
CARRIZOZO — The Lincoln County Detention Center is operating without a health care provider while at least two inmates are on suicide watch and several others take psychiatric medication, according to a jail staff member.

The staff member, who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation, also alleges that the warden overruled a medical decision this past weekend to send an inmate to the hospital.

According to the staff member, the jail’s medical provider determined over the weekend that an inmate needed hospital care. The warden said the situation was not an emergency and did not want to incur another bill, so the inmate was not taken to the hospital, the staff member said. The provider’s last day at the jail was Monday.

“I don’t think it is legal to operate without health care,” the staff member said.

Inmates on suicide watch and psychiatric holds require medication and medical monitoring, the staff member said, and corrections officers are not qualified to give medication and make assessments.

Alamogordo Town News is not identifying the inmates in order to protect their privacy.

The allegations come one week after the jail let go a nurse who had said she feared for her safety and refused to give medications without proper procedures and protections in place, according to multiple sources.

Alamogordo Town News previously reported on a recent suicide at the jail and then another recent attempt. The newspaper has filed a request under the state Inspection of Public Records Act seeking records on staffing levels and on allegations that the jail is being managed to turn a profit and is in final stages of renewal of a contract with Lincoln County. 

The detention center is a [148]-bed facility in Carrizozo operated under contract by Correctional Solutions Group LLC. 

New Mexico laws are ambiguous in requiring county jails to employ full time a medical provider. However, jails are constitutionally required to provide adequate medical care to people in their custody, and courts have found that ignoring requests for medical help or delaying emergency care can amount to deliberate indifference.

Contracting jail operations to a private company does not end the county’s responsibility. A federal court has ruled that a New Mexico county that keeps oversight of its privately run jail can still be held liable for unconstitutional practices adopted by the contractor. State law also allows a county to end its contract with a private jail operator that fails to meet the minimum standards of incarceration written into that contract.

An email has been sent to county leadership and the Lincoln County Sheriff’s office for comment.

item.title: Regional Arts and Culture: Roswell Symphony Orchestra Opens Season With America 250, Featuring Gershwin’s “Porgy and Bess”
item.description:
ROSWELL, NM — The Roswell Symphony Orchestra is back from summer break and preparing a tribute to the country’s 250th anniversary to launch its latest musical season.

On Sept. 26, the RSO will present America 250, a concert program honoring the signing of the Declaration of Independence with patriotic pieces from various eras. Audiences can look forward to hearing compositions by Aaron Copland, George Gershwin, Leroy Anderson and John Philip Sousa, plus a medley of U.S. military branch songs and an invitation to sing along with the symphony to an arrangement of “America, the Beautiful.”

The Gershwin portion of the program features selections from “Porgy and Bess,” which the composer called a “folk opera” when it premiered in 1935. The work blended classical composition with jazz, blues and spirituals in a way that was new at the time, and many of its melodies became standards in their own right, including “Summertime,” “I Got Plenty o’ Nuttin’,” “It Ain’t Necessarily So” and “Bess, You Is My Woman Now.”

Set in Charleston, South Carolina’s fictional Catfish Row, the opera follows love, hardship and hope in a tight-knit community, with a score that ranges from tender lullabies to joyful, soaring moments.

RSO Music Director Dr. John Farrer described the anniversary as a once-in-a-lifetime milestone, calling the concert “our chance to celebrate this very special occasion.” He said the program is made up of enjoyable, beautiful, well-composed and accessible music, and that he and the orchestra will be having a good time as well.

The concert begins at 7 p.m., a new start time for the orchestra. It will be held at Pearson Auditorium, 101 W. College Blvd., on the New Mexico Military Institute campus. Tickets are available at roswellsymphony.org, by calling 575-623-5882 or at the door, and range from $20 to $35. Students attend all symphony concerts free of charge.

The rest of the season

After the season opener, the RSO has three more concerts on the calendar:

• Christmas Classics — Sunday, Dec. 13, 2026, at 2:30 p.m., a holiday matinee.• Classical and Romantic — Saturday, March 6, 2027, at 7 p.m., with guest violin soloist Nathan Meltzer featured on the Mozart Violin Concerto.• Rhapsody in Blue — Saturday, April 24, 2027, at 7 p.m., featuring Gershwin’s “Rhapsody in Blue” with returning guest piano soloist Evren Ozel.

“I think the rest of the season will be absolutely terrific,” Farrer says.

About the RSO

The orchestra traces its roots to the basement of the First Methodist Church, where it first gathered on July 28, 1959. That original group was made up of lawyers, accountants, teachers, florists, housewives and geologists — amateurs determined to give the region a professional-sounding orchestra. Farrer took the podium for the 1972 season, following William Kirschke, Thomas Lewis and founding director Glenn Cunningham. He is a recipient of the Governor’s Award for Excellence and Achievement.

Today the orchestra’s professional musicians travel from cities within a 200-mile radius of Roswell, including Lubbock, Amarillo, Santa Fe, Albuquerque, Las Cruces, El Paso, Portales and Alamogordo. Its mission is to bring the best of orchestral literature to Roswell and Southeast New Mexico through an annual concert season and music education programs for children and young adults.

If you go

WHAT: Roswell Symphony Orchestra presents America 250

WHEN: Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026, at 7 p.m.

WHERE: Pearson Auditorium, 101 W. College Blvd., Roswell, NM 88201

TICKETS: $20–$35 at roswellsymphony.org, 575-623-5882 or at the door; students free

item.title: Alamogordo Goes Black & Gold for AHS Homecoming Week
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Alamogordo High School Homecoming Week kicks off Sept. 28, and Alamogordo Public Schools is asking the entire community to help turn the town Black & Gold through Oct. 3.

Residents are encouraged to decorate homes, storefronts and vehicles in school colors, and local businesses can request free marketing kits to join the celebration. Registration for Friday's Homecoming Parade is now open.

A full week of Tiger athletics

The district is urging fans to turn out all week long. Boys Soccer and Volleyball take the field Tuesday. On Wednesday, the Powder Fluff and Powder Puff games will raise money for the junior and senior classes, with tickets just $2 cash at the gate. Girls Soccer plays Thursday.

The week peaks Friday, Oct. 2, with the Homecoming Parade at 3 p.m., followed by the Homecoming football game against Mayfield at 7 p.m. at Tiger Stadium.

Season passes covering all sports at all levels are available now, and individual game tickets can be purchased on the APS website or through the Hometown Tickets app. Admission to regular-season events is free for APS staff, APS students and children 5 and under.

Alumni coming home

The classes of 1986, 1996 and 2006 are holding reunions during Homecoming Week, with plans that include attending Friday's game.

The district is also promoting its new Spotlight on Alumni program, which highlights AHS graduates making a difference, from local entrepreneurs to doctors, engineers and educators around the world. Graduates, or anyone who knows a Tiger doing great things, can share a story through a short online form in the newsletter. Questions can be sent to communications@alamogordoschools.org.

Tiger heads to Grand Canyon

Adding to the week's pride, AHS softball standout Khloe Lunar has committed to continue her career at Grand Canyon University. A pitcher, outfielder and first baseman, Lunar is known as a natural leader on a team that doesn't name an official captain. She said GCU's program, team culture, campus and proximity to her grandparents sealed the decision.

"Softball has taught me that the biggest part of the journey isn't where you play, but the people you become along the way," Lunar said.

More information

Parade registration, business kit requests and the full home-game schedule are available in the APS Homecoming Newsletter at app.smore.com/n/5196px. Athletic calendars and printable schedules are on the APS website. For questions, call or text the APS Call Center at 575-812-8573 during business hours, or use the district's 24/7 chatbot.

item.title: New Mexico Supreme Court Law Library Named Best in the Nation
item.description:
SANTA FE, N.M. — Sept. 22, 2026 — The U.S. Government Publishing Office (GPO) has named the New Mexico Supreme Court Law Library in Santa Fe the 2026 Federal Depository Library of the Year, the top national honor for libraries that give the public free access to federal government information.

The award was presented virtually during the Federal Depository Library Conference in Washington, D.C. State Law Librarian and Depository Coordinator Stephanie Wilson accepted the honor from the Law Library in Santa Fe.

GPO said the library was selected for its exceptional commitment to providing free public access to government information, preserving its collection, and serving communities throughout New Mexico. GPO Director Hugh Nathanial Halpern said the library "demonstrates the vital role Federal Depository Libraries play in connecting people with Government information."

Wilson said the library "preserves, promotes and provides access to public records and legal information," a mission it has carried out since it was established as New Mexico's Territorial Library in 1851. She noted that staff respond to every request from people who walk in, call, mail, or email for help with legal research, court forms, document delivery, and other information, and thanked GPO for recognizing the library's work.

A small staff with a big mission

For more than 175 years, the library has served New Mexico's judiciary, government, legal community, and public. Today it maintains a research collection of more than 300,000 items and serves a wide range of patrons, from judges and attorneys to self-represented litigants and curious residents.

A staff of five provides reference help in person and by phone, email, and mail. Much of that work draws on the library's federal government information collection, which librarians use to answer both current and historical questions about federal law, and to guide patrons through tangible and electronic government resources.

Why print still matters in New Mexico

New Mexico is the fifth-largest state by area, and many of its communities sit in technology deserts with limited or unreliable internet access. For that reason, the Law Library deliberately selects and preserves core legal resources in print, including the Code of Federal Regulations, the United States Code, and United States Reports, so patrons can reach the law whether or not they can get online. The library also rarely weeds its collection, supporting long-term access and preservation.

Making the collection easier to find

Library staff recently completed an item-level inventory of more than 11,900 items in the library's SuDocs collection. SuDocs, short for Superintendent of Documents, is a specialized classification system used to organize U.S. federal government publications. Librarians have also been adding federal depository resources to the online catalog, making them easier for the public to discover.

Reaching the public beyond the building

Over the past year, staff have led more than 40 tours of the Law Library and taken part in numerous legal fairs, helping New Mexicans learn what resources exist and how to use them.

About the Federal Depository Library Program

GPO produces and distributes information products for all three branches of the federal government, including U.S. passports and the official publications of Congress, the White House, and federal agencies. It provides free, permanent public access to federal information through GovInfo.gov and partnerships with about 1,100 libraries nationwide in the Federal Depository Library Program.

item.title: Alamogordo Commission Drops Conduct Complaint Against Hernandez on a Split Vote, Awards Golf Course Contract
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The Alamogordo City Commission on Tuesday declined to move forward with a code of conduct complaint against Commissioner Alfonso Hernandez, ending the matter after a 2-4 vote.

Under the city's code of conduct, the complaint was first reviewed by legal counsel and then referred to the commission's three senior members, who each ruled on whether the allegations were founded. City Manager Robert Stockwell told the commission that two of the three found the allegations unfounded and one found them founded, which sent the question of further action to the full commission.

A motion by Commissioner Baxter Patillo, seconded by Commissioner Warren Robinson, to take further action and schedule an open hearing failed with two votes in favor and four against. The two votes in favor of a hearing to review his actions were by Commissioner Warren Robinson and Mayor Sharon McDonald. As expected the gang of Hernandez members led by Josh Rardin, Potillo, Burnett and Tapley opposed any public disciplinary hearing. Hernandez stepped out of the meeting before the item and did not vote.

Hear a commentary on the process and thoughts from the outside by former City Manager Dr Hernandez:

See related story:  City Leadership Gives Two Different Accounts of How the Al Hernandez Complaint Was Handled

Golf course goes to private management

Commissioners voted 6-0, with one abstention, to authorize contract negotiations with Maxim Golf Solutions LLC to run the Desert Lakes Golf Course, including the pro shop, clubhouse, restaurant and course maintenance.

Heather Casbolt, introduced Tuesday as the city's new Parks and Recreation director, said the city received two proposals. A five-member evaluation committee scored Maxim higher in all five categories, giving it a final score of 81.6, with its strongest marks in course operations and maintenance.

Mayor Sharon McDonald asked questions concerning rather there was a cap on the golf course subsidies to maintain the golf course. Stockwell said the city's golf subsidy has averaged roughly $260,000 a year and has at times run much higher. The contractor will operate and maintain city-owned equipment, while the city remains responsible for replacing worn-out items. Casbolt said a new fleet of 45 golf carts and seven or eight utility vehicles, purchased from Yamaha through Sourcewell, is expected between mid-October and mid-November.

The contract has drawn objections from city employees. Tamara Hanson, president of the union local representing city workers, told commissioners the union filed a grievance over the golf course request for proposals on Sept. 2 and is still awaiting a resolution. She also said contractors hired to work on the course had twice damaged it in the past week, including newly installed irrigation rotors.

Bonito Lake stays open for fishing, for now

Several residents urged the commission to keep Bonito Lake open to the public. Lori Armstrong, chair of the city's Parks and Recreation Board, asked commissioners to preserve access and to consult the board earlier on recreation decisions, saying they are too often fast-tracked. Lifelong resident Enrique Tels said the lake is one of the few cool-weather fishing spots within reach and that money for fencing would be better spent on city streets.

Stockwell recommended three steps. First, the commission would reaffirm that the lake's top priority is as a water source for Alamogordo and Holloman Air Force Base, with recreation secondary. Second, the city would keep the lake open for fishing under its current agreement with the state and make immediate improvements to shoreline access. Third, the city would work with Lincoln County, Ruidoso, Ruidoso Downs and the state on long-term options and report back within six months. A question was posed rather Holloman had been consulted in the process and Mr Stockwell danced around the response and said they just want it protected as a water source. The mayor of Ruidoso Downs and the small business owner of Bonito Bait and Tackle was also present to support keeping the lake open to the public. 

There was confusion by Mr Stockwell on rather a vote should be taken. Because the item was posted only as commission direction, no formal vote was taken. Commissioners gave consensus support to the plan.

Asked about recent rains, Stockwell said detention basins built after the wildfires caught a substantial amount of debris that would otherwise have reached the lake. He warned the threat remains as burned trees continue to fall, and said any future recreation must not interfere with debris control.

Residents seek help on PNM bills

She read accounts from customers, including a mother of six facing a $1,200 demand. Jeanie Nichols, who lives south of Tularosa, said her September bill was four times her usual amount.

item.title: Commentary: Chalk Another One Up for the Good Ole Boys
item.description:
Alamogordo N. M. - Tuesday night in Alamogordo, justice didn't lose a fight. It never got into the ring.

By a 2-4 vote, the City Commission declined to hold a public hearing on the code of conduct complaint filed against Commissioner Alfonso "Al" Hernandez. Only Mayor Sharon McDonald and Commissioner Warren Robinson voted to let the matter see daylight. As predicted, Commissioners Josh Rardin, Baxter Patillo, Stephen Burnett and Mark Tapley made sure it wouldn't. Under the city code, that's the end of it. No hearing. No findings. No further action. Ever.

And here's the part that should make every voter in Alamogordo sit up. The motion to hold that hearing was made by Commissioner Patillo himself, who then turned around and voted against it.

Patillo put the question on the table only to help knock it off. If that was meant to look like fairness, it didn't fool anyone watching. It looked like theater, a way to say the question was asked while making sure it was never answered.

Supporters of the vote will say the process was followed. That is exactly the problem.

The process is the scandal.

Here's what happened. A city employee filed the first complaint ever processed under Section 2-03-570 of the municipal code. The code says the City Attorney screens it first. Alamogordo hasn't had a City Attorney since May. So the job went to Darrell Mori, the former City Attorney, who left with a settlement and now works for the city on contract. And by the city's own account, he didn't investigate anything. He checked whether the paperwork was filled out correctly.

Even the story of that step kept shifting. On Monday, City Manager Robert Stockwell told Alamogordo Town News the entire matter was handled by Mori. By Tuesday morning, under further questioning, the account changed: Mori only confirmed the complaint met the filing requirements, because the code doesn't call for an investigation. Two different explanations in less than 24 hours, from the man responsible for running the city.

From there, the complaint went to three of Hernandez's own colleagues on the commission. Two found no cause. One found cause on all four counts. The public still hasn't been told which commissioners sat on that panel, how each voted, or even what the allegations are. Then the full commission, which  included the very members who had already cleared him, voted on whether anyone should look any further. They said no. An in depth IPRA has been filed to secure more details and legal counsel has been consulted in the event of stonewalling by the city.

Think about that. Nobody independent ever examined the facts. Nobody asked the question that matters: did it happen.

The accused commissioner's peers, some of them his reliable allies on the dais, simply decided the question shouldn't be asked in public.

When Stockwell was asked whether this was a sound way to handle misconduct complaints, he called it "a discussion for another time."

For the employee who filed this complaint, there is no other time. The door is closed. 

Except it’s not completely closed, she could file a complaint of harassment under title 7 with HR and eventually the courts. The city’s failure to even open an investigation and public inquiry does not bold well for a positive outcome to the city if lawsuits are eventually filed. 

And this isn't a matter of personnel secrecy. Hernandez is an elected official, not a city employee. New Mexico's public records and open meetings laws draw a real line between protecting employees and shielding officials from scrutiny over conduct in office. Voters have every right to know what their representatives are accused of and how it was handled.

Contrast this with 2023 and 2025, when the city paid for outside investigations into complaints involving commissioners and the city manager hiring process. Stockwell calls that comparison apples to oranges because those weren't filed under this code section. Maybe so. But the public sees the fruit either way: when accountability is inconvenient for the majority, the rules somehow never require it.

At public comment, Kim Great White Owl Morello of Alamogordo Voters for Accountability told commissioners they seemed "willing to discipline the wrong people." Tuesday's vote did nothing to prove her wrong.

This is how the good ole boy system works. Nobody breaks the rules. The rules are just written so the people in power never have to answer.

A contract lawyer checks a form. Friends review a friend. A commissioner makes a motion and votes it down. The majority looks away. Everyone goes home, and the complaint dies without a single fact being tested.

If Commissioner Hernandez did nothing wrong, a public hearing would have cleared his name. Four commissioners, showing a lack of ethics and integrity decided the town didn't deserve to find out either way.

Alamogordo deserves a code of conduct and a charter with teeth: independent review, public findings, and a process that doesn't let colleagues grade each other's homework. Until then, every resident should remember how this vote went, and who cast it, when election season comes around.

Because justice didn't fail on its own Tuesday night. It had help.

item.title: State Police make arrests in Guadalupe County shooting, Albuquerque stolen-vehicle chase
item.description:
UADALUPE COUNTY, N.M. — New Mexico State Police made arrests in two separate cases last week: a 22-year-old man accused of stealing two vehicles and shooting his ex-girlfriend in Guadalupe County, and three juveniles who police say fled from a stolen vehicle carrying a loaded handgun in Albuquerque.

Riel Gonzales faces 13 charges after the Saturday, Sept. 19, incident, which left both him and his 18-year-old ex-girlfriend with gunshot wounds.

State police say it began at about 11:10 a.m. at the Phillips 66 Milagro gas station at 1095 Russell Road, where Gonzales and the woman had been in a reported domestic dispute.

According to the preliminary investigation, the woman left in a black BMW. Gonzales then allegedly stole a red Dykon Blasting work truck while its driver was pumping gas and followed her toward Anton Chico.

Police say the woman drove to a home, where Gonzales allegedly left the work truck, took her BMW and drove off. Her mother arrived soon after and picked her up.

As the mother and daughter left the area, they came upon Gonzales on NM 119. At some point shots were fired and a vehicle crash occurred, police said.

The mother's boyfriend, who was driving to the scene, saw what happened. Police say Gonzales fired at him as he arrived but missed. The boyfriend got out of his vehicle, shot Gonzales and held him down until officers arrived and took him into custody.

The woman was shot in the left arm and Gonzales in the right arm. Both were taken to an area hospital. The woman was later moved to a hospital in Texas, where she was treated and released.

Gonzales was booked into the Colfax County Detention Center on a probation hold. The Fourth Judicial District Attorney's Office approved charges including aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, four counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, possession of a firearm by a felon, shooting at or from a motor vehicle, two counts of unlawful taking of a motor vehicle, three counts of criminal damage to property over $1,000, and interference with communications.

The NMSP Investigations Bureau is still investigating.

Two days earlier, on Thursday, Sept. 17, agents with the NMSP Crime Suppression Bureau found a stolen vehicle near Southern Avenue and Utah Street in Albuquerque. The driver fled from agents but soon reached a dead-end street, where agents boxed in the vehicle.

Four people then ran from the vehicle on foot. Agents caught three, including the driver. The fourth was not found despite a perimeter search and the use of a drone.

Inside the vehicle, agents found a Glock handgun with an extended magazine holding 23 rounds, along with a Glock-style replica BB or pellet gun whose magazine held three live 9 mm rounds.

The three juveniles were booked into the Juvenile Detention Center on charges of aggravated fleeing of a law enforcement officer, unlawful possession of a firearm by a person under 19, receiving or transferring a stolen motor vehicle, and resisting, evading or obstructing an officer. Their names were not released because they are minors.

item.title: Court Win for CNN, Politico and MS NOW Leaves Smaller Newsrooms Asking: Who Defends Us?
item.description:
WASHINGTON — A federal judge early Thursday ordered the White House to restore access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico, temporarily blocking President Donald Trump's ban on the three outlets. Independent publishers and local newsrooms say the fight has implications well beyond the briefing room.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a 14-day temporary restraining order, finding the outlets were likely to prove their press passes were pulled without due process. Kelly, a Trump appointee who restored a CNN reporter's credentials in a similar 2018 dispute, also said the White House needs clear rules for what conduct can cost a journalist their pass. He called the standard in the administration's letters to the outlets "so vague it hardly does the trick."

Trump announced the ban last Friday, first calling the outlets "fake news" and later arguing that their reporting posed a national security risk. In a joint lawsuit, the outlets said they were being punished for the content of their coverage, a core First Amendment violation. Their attorney, Theodore Boutrous Jr., praised the ruling as a win for press freedom and the rule of law. The White House did not immediately comment.

A fight most newsrooms couldn't afford

The three outlets won quickly because they could move quickly. They had a nationally known First Amendment litigator, a joint legal strategy and the resources to get a hearing within days. Most of the country's newsrooms have none of that.

Local papers, public radio stations and independent digital outlets often run on thin budgets with no in-house lawyer. When a public utility office fails to respond to IPRA requests, a sheriff ignores press inquiries, or a school board shuts a critical outlet in responses, many small newsrooms simply absorb the loss. For Alamogordo Town News legal reporter advise is our second largest expense. 

Press freedom advocates have long warned that exclusion tactics tested at the national level tend to spread. The White House has already clashed with the Associated Press over Oval Office access and taken control of which outlets join the rotating press pool, a role long managed by the White House Correspondents' Association. Many smaller and regional outlets relied on that pool system for their only direct view of the presidency.

Why the ruling still matters locally

Kelly's reasoning could be useful to local journalists even though it only binds this case. His emphasis on due process and clear, content-neutral standards echoes principles that reporters can raise when a city hall or state agency ignores press inquiries.

Groups such as the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press offer free legal help to journalists facing access fights, and some states have press associations that do the same. Local editors say many reporters don't know those resources exist until they need them.

What comes next

The order lasts two weeks, and the government can seek to extend the dispute or appeal. For now, reporters from the three outlets can return to the White House grounds.

For newsrooms without national reach, the lesson may be less about this outcome than about preparation. Access, they say, is easiest to defend when a legal plan is in place before it's taken away. Alamogordo Town News stays vigilant in protecting press access and the use of IPRA and Open Meetings Act access to ensure local media access and transparency to the public.

item.title: Lecture Offers a Virtual Journey Through Historic Cairo and Ancient Egypt
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Local audiences can tour the pyramids, temples and royal tombs of Egypt without leaving southern New Mexico when David Greenwald of the Jornada Research Institute presents "Historic Cairo and Ancient Nile Explorations" on Tuesday, Oct. 20, at the Otero Artspace.

The free-standing lecture, part of the Otero Arts and Jornada Research Institute Lecture Series, begins at 6:30 p.m. Doors open at 6 p.m. The Otero Artspace is at 1118 Indiana Ave., at the corner of 12th Street and Indiana Avenue.

The presentation previews the Jornada Research Institute's Overseas Journeys Program trip to Egypt, which Greenwald will lead later in October and November. Attendees will follow the planned route as Greenwald describes each historic site and monument the tour group will visit.

The journey begins at Giza, with the Great Pyramids, the Great Sphinx and the wider Giza Necropolis, including a look inside the Pyramid of Khufu. From there the talk moves to Saqqara, home of the Step Pyramid and its mortuary complex, much of which has recently been opened to visitors.

The route then shifts south to Aswan and Abu Simbel, where Greenwald will discuss the massive salvage operation that relocated the Temple of Ramesses II and the Temple of Hathor and Nefertari to save them from rising waters. From the Aswan Dam, the group travels north by ship down the Nile to Luxor, stopping at temples dedicated to pharaohs who became historical legends, along with their elaborate tombs.

At ancient Thebes, the center of Egyptian power and a landscape of major temple building, the talk explores the Valley of the Kings and the Valley of the Queens, the burial grounds of Egypt's royal families for roughly 500 years. Greenwald will use the site to explain Egypt's decline at the end of the Bronze Age, around 1150 B.C., the later rise of the Ptolemaic Dynasty and Egypt's eventual absorption into the Roman Empire.

The presentation closes with a brief look at the spread of Christianity in Egypt and the era of Islamic rule in Cairo, including a visit to the medieval Citadel of Saladin.

Greenwald is affiliated with the Jornada Research Institute, which co-sponsors the lecture series with Otero Arts.

item.title: Jury to resume deliberations Friday in New Mexico's Cambridge Analytica case against Facebook
item.description:
SANTA FE — A Santa Fe jury went home Thursday without reaching a verdict in State of New Mexico, et al. v. Facebook, Inc., and will resume deliberations at 9 a.m. Friday, according to a media advisory from Barry Massey, chief communications officer for the Administrative Office of the Courts.

The case centers on Facebook's role in the Cambridge Analytica scandal. The state alleges that Meta Platforms failed to protect the personal data of Facebook users or effectively curtail the spread of hate speech and misinformation on the platform. The state estimates roughly 350,000 New Mexicans were among the U.S. Facebook users whose data the now-defunct London consulting firm harvested — a number that likely includes residents of Otero County.

What jurors must decide

Jurors must weigh the truthfulness of 34 statements made by Meta and decide whether the company violated New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act, a consumer protection law aimed at deceptive or "unconscionable" business practices. The state is seeking the maximum civil penalties under the act, up to $5,000 per violation, along with an injunction to halt future breaches of user data.

The lawsuit dates to 2021. It was filed by then-Attorney General Hector Balderas as part of a wave of state privacy suits after 2018 reports that Facebook had allowed Cambridge Analytica to harvest data from up to 87 million Americans for use in 2016 political campaigns. New Mexico declined to join a multistate Meta settlement and chose to pursue its own litigation.

Closing arguments

Testimony began Sept. 9 in 1st Judicial District Court before Judge Francis Mathew, and closing arguments wrapped up Wednesday afternoon. The trial featured testimony from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and former Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg, both of whom addressed the company's response to the Cambridge Analytica revelations.

State attorney Randi McGinn told jurors Meta's leaders made false promises about protecting users' data. "Does lying matter anymore in America?" she asked in closing.

Meta attorney Dane Butswinkas countered that the case rests on a breach more than a decade old and ignores safeguards the company has put in place since. He also argued the Unfair Practices Act doesn't apply because Facebook is a free service with no sale, rental, lease or loan involved.

Third showdown this year

This is the third time in 2026 that New Mexico and Meta have faced off in a Santa Fe courtroom. In March, a jury ordered Meta to pay $375 million in civil penalties in a case brought by Attorney General Raúl Torrez over child safety on its platforms, and in August, Judge Bryan Biedscheid ordered Meta to pay $567 million into a youth mental health abatement fund after declaring the platform's design a public nuisance. Meta has said it disagrees with the March verdict and will appeal.

The 2nd Life Media Alamogordo Town News will report the verdict once it is announced.

item.title: Sept 29, Noon to 2 pm: PRC to Hear From PNM Customers Over Estimated Readings and Delayed Bills at Alamogordo Town Hall
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — PNM customers who have received unexpectedly high or late electric bills this summer will get a chance to tell state regulators directly. The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission (NMPRC), which oversees investor-owned utilities including PNM, is holding a community town hall on Tuesday, Sept. 29, from noon to 2 p.m. at the Sgt. Willie Estrada Memorial Civic Center in Alamogordo. The event will also be livestreamed online.

Customers are encouraged to bring copies of their bills and share their experiences. The commission says public input will help it better understand local impacts and ensure appropriate corrective actions are implemented.

How the problem started

The billing trouble traces back to a shortage of PNM meter readers. The issue began in Alamogordo in July before spreading statewide in August. With fewer workers available to read meters, PNM issued more estimated bills, and some customers received their bills late. Some of those estimated bills reached as high as $1,000, prompting customer complaints and questions from the New Mexico Department of Justice.

The PRC's Consumer Relations Division and Public Interest Advocacy Staff met with PNM to understand what caused the estimated readings, including staffing and meter-reading challenges, and what steps were being taken to fix them. PNM initially told the state that customers should expect estimated bills through October.

What an estimated bill means

PNM calculates estimated readings using an account's usage from the previous month and the same month a year earlier. If the estimate is too high or too low, it is corrected on a later "true-up" bill once an actual reading is taken. Under NMPRC rules, PNM may estimate residential readings for no more than two consecutive months. Customers can check whether their bill was estimated by looking at the "Meter read type" on page two of the bill.

For some households, delayed bills meant paying for two months at once. PNM apologized to customers by email, said it was bringing in meter readers from other parts of the state, and noted payment plans may be available to those billed for two months in one cycle.

PNM says it has caught up

PNM spokesperson Eric Chavez said the utility has essentially caught up on missed readings and does not expect further estimates or missed reads, though the company could not say how many new meter readers it has hired. PNM also said it did not lay off Alamogordo meter readers and is looking for new roles for them as it transitions to smart meters.

Other ways to get help

Customers who need help can contact the NMPRC's Consumer Relations Division, which can connect them with PNM through an informal complaint process. A formal complaint option is available if issues can't be resolved informally. Filings in the matter can be reviewed on the PRCe360 portal under case number 26‑0000147. Customers can also reach PNM directly at 888-DIAL-PNM.

item.title: Alamogordo Invited to Welcome Home Veteran Larry Sanmann From Honor Flight
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Alamogordo is invited — and challenged — to fill VFW Post 7686 on Saturday night and welcome home Air Force veteran Larry Sanmann as he returns from Washington, D.C., with Rio Grande Honor Flight Mission 22.

The homecoming, hosted by the U.S. Veterans Motorcycle Club, Trinity Chapter, with the Patriot Guard Riders, begins at 7 p.m. Organizers are asking the public to bring American flags, welcome home banners and all the patriotism they can carry, giving Sanmann the hometown welcome many Vietnam veterans never received.

It is a fitting salute to a man whose working life was measured in turbine blades and the roar of jet engines. From the flight lines of Vietnam to the hangars at Holloman Air Force Base, Sanmann spent more than three decades keeping some of America's most storied aircraft in the air.

From Nebraska to Vietnam

Sanmann enlisted in the Air Force in 1967 from his hometown of McCool Junction, Nebraska, and trained as a jet engine mechanic. His first assignment was Cannon Air Force Base in Clovis, but his stay in eastern New Mexico was a short one.

Before long he was at Phan Rang Air Base in South Vietnam, where he served from 1968 to 1969. There he maintained the jet engines of the F-100 Super Sabre, the fighter-bomber that flew close air support missions throughout the war.

Engines around the world

After Vietnam, Sanmann was assigned to Tinker Air Force Base in Oklahoma, where most of the Air Force's jet engines went for depot-level overhaul and maintenance. There he worked on just about every jet engine the service was flying at the time.

His next stop was McConnell Air Force Base in Kansas, working on the Pratt & Whitney J57 engines of the KC-135 Stratotanker, the workhorse of aerial refueling and cargo airlift. From McConnell he deployed to Andersen Air Force Base on Guam in 1972 in support of Operation Bullet Shot, the massive buildup of B-52 Stratofortress bombers in the Pacific during the Vietnam War. On Guam he kept the B-52s' engines running.

Sanmann then moved to Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, Japan, where he continued maintaining KC-135 engines. From there he was stationed at Hill Air Force Base in Utah, working on the engines of the F-4 Phantom II and the F-16 Fighting Falcon.

Home at Holloman

His final Air Force assignment brought him back to New Mexico, to Holloman Air Force Base, where he closed out his career working on the F-15 Eagle. Sanmann retired after 21 years of active duty at the rank of master sergeant (E-7).

Retirement didn't last long. As Sanmann tells it, he simply walked across the flight line and took a job with DynCorp maintaining T-38 Talons — and, once again, their jet engines. He later worked on the German Air Force's F-4 Phantoms and their engines at Holloman until 2004, when he retired a second time, "so he says."

To keep from getting bored, he then drove the shuttle between Alamogordo and Holloman. Today Sanmann is fully retired and makes his permanent home in Alamogordo.

This weekend he will travel with Honor Flight Mission 22 to Washington, D.C., organized by Rio Grande Honor Flight, to visit the memorials built in honor of those who served. After a lifetime spent keeping America's aircraft flying, he says he is looking forward to it.

If you go

Join the welcome home celebration for Larry Sanmann:

• When: Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026, at 7 p.m.• Where: VFW Post 7686, 700 Highway 70 West, Alamogordo• Hosted by: U.S. Veterans Motorcycle Club, Trinity Chapter, with the Patriot Guard Riders and Rio Grande Honor Flight

Bring your flags, your banners and a friend. Sanmann gave 21 years in uniform and decades more on the flight line — it takes one evening to tell him thank you.

item.title: Lady Tigers Outlast Ruidoso in Five-Set Thriller
item.description:
Alamogordo closes the match on an 8-0 run to beat Ruidoso; Tularosa falls to Quemado.

It took all five sets and every ounce of energy the Lady Tigers had, but Alamogordo pulled away from Ruidoso when it mattered most, winning 27-25, 14-25, 25-15, 24-26, 15-6.

The win improves Alamogordo to 5-7 on the season.

The opening set set the tone. Neither team could pull away, and it took extra points before Alamogordo finally closed it out 27-25.

The Lady Tigers looked ready to build on that momentum early in the second set, jumping out to a 9-4 lead. Ruidoso answered emphatically. The Warriors took a 12-11 lead, stretched it to 18-12 and outscored Alamogordo 21-5 after trailing 9-4 to win the set 25-14 and even the match at 1-1.

Alamogordo responded with its most dominant set of the night. The Lady Tigers led 8-3, then 15-5 and 19-11 before cruising to a 25-15 win and a 2-1 match lead.

The fourth set looked headed the same direction. Alamogordo led 10-5 and still held a 15-13 edge midway through, but Ruidoso rallied to take a 23-20 lead. The Lady Tigers fought back to force extra points, but Ruidoso escaped 26-24 to tie the match 2-2 and force a deciding fifth set.

With the match on the line, Alamogordo took control early, scoring the first three points of the fifth set. Ruidoso clawed back within 7-6, but that was as close as the Warriors would get. The Lady Tigers scored the final eight points of the match to win the set 15-6 and seal the victory.

Alamogordo is back in action Saturday at Socorro.

In other area action, Tularosa fell to Quemado in straight sets.

The loss drops the Lady Cats to 3-8 on the season. Tularosa returns home Tuesday to host Hatch Valley.

Alamogordo NM- Artesia pulled away from Alamogordo on Friday, scoring 35 unanswered points after the Tigers cut the lead to two early in the third quarter, for a 54-19 win.

Artesia led 14-0 after the first quarter behind Logan Rodriguez, who threw a 62-yard touchdown pass to Layton Whitmire and ran for a 9-yard score. Alamogordo quarterback Nathanael Cereceres answered with a 14-yard touchdown run, and Russell's extra point made it 14-7. After Lucas Atkins hit Whitmire on a 4-yard touchdown pass, Cereceres found Aiden Rowe for a 31-yard score with 1:25 left in the half, sending the Tigers into halftime down 21-13.

Bryson Bloom opened the second half with a 67-yard touchdown run to pull Alamogordo within 21-19, but the two-point try to tie was no good. Artesia took over from there. Atkins threw touchdown passes of 35 yards to Kai Greathouse and 44 yards to Tyler Egeland, Rodriguez added a 40-yard run, Derek Ruiz returned an interception 30 yards for a score, and Chance Hocker tossed a 4-yard touchdown to Andres Ortiz to close out the scoring.

Tigers drop to 2-4, 1-2 in district – host Mayfield next Friday.
